analysis.one_liner: Bans unconscionably high fuel prices during declared energy emergencies, with fines funding low-income heating aid.
analysis.headline: The House passed the anti-gouging bill 284-141 on May 23, 2007, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to charge unconscionably excessive prices for gasoline and other fuels at wholesale or retail during a declared energy emergency. It would let the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general sue violators, with civil fines up to triple the illicit profits and criminal fines up to $150 million for corporations. Money collected in fines would go to a fund for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay heating bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and other fuel buyers, who would be protected from price spikes during hurricanes, supply disruptions, and other declared emergencies; state attorneys general, who would get a new federal tool to sue on behalf of their residents; and low-income households, who would receive heating assistance funded by penalties collected from violators.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful, during a presidentially declared energy emergency, to sell gasoline or other petroleum distillates at wholesale or retail at a price that is unconscionably excessive or takes unfair advantage of the emergency.

Gives the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforcement power: civil fines of up to three times the violator's profits or $3 million, and criminal fines up to $150 million for corporations or $2 million and 10 years for individuals, with the FTC instructed to prioritize companies with over $500 million in annual fuel sales.
Allows a state, acting on behalf of its residents, to sue in federal court over retail price gouging, and states that nothing in the bill preempts stronger state laws.
Requires all fines and penalties collected to go into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund that pays for Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) heating aid for low-income households.

Makes it unlawful to knowingly report false wholesale price information to a federal agency, with a civil penalty up to $1 million, and directs the FTC to promote price transparency in wholesale fuel markets.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, refiners, fuel wholesalers, and retail sellers, who would face civil fines of up to triple their excess profits, corporate criminal fines up to $150 million, and lawsuits by state attorneys general when they charge unconscionably excessive prices during declared emergencies.

drawbacks.text: The ban only applies after the President declares an energy emergency covering a specific area and fuel, with each declaration limited to 30 days at a time, so high pump prices outside a declared emergency are untouched — a much narrower bill than the version introduced in February 2007, which covered crude oil and natural gas at all times and banned wholesale market manipulation.
Transactions on futures markets are expressly excluded from the prohibition, leaving speculation in fuel futures outside the bill's reach.

Because sellers face fines for prices deemed unconscionably excessive, critics of gouging laws argue that suppliers may hesitate to rush extra fuel into an emergency area, which could worsen shortages; the bill tries to counter this by letting courts consider whether a seller's price reflected added costs and risks and whether the seller actually increased supply.

The standard — 'unconscionably excessive' pricing that takes 'unfair advantage' — is subjective and would invite litigation over exactly when a legitimate price response to a shortage becomes illegal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the benefit is real but limited: protection from emergency price spikes, paid for by the companies that create them, with penalties recycled into heating aid. The honest costs are that the bill as passed is far narrower than what was proposed — it needs a presidential proclamation, covers only gasoline and petroleum distillates, exempts futures trading, and hinges on a vague 'unconscionably excessive' standard — and that emergency price caps can, in theory, dull sellers' incentive to move fuel into a hard-hit area. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection whose design flaws limit but do not erase its value.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the Federal Price Gouging Prevention Act on February 28, 2007, and it drew 125 cosponsors, 122 of them Democrats.

The version introduced in February 2007 covered crude oil, gasoline, natural gas, and petroleum distillates at any time, banned false wholesale price reporting and market manipulation, and directed the FTC to promote wholesale price transparency.

The version the House passed on May 23, 2007 was much narrower: the unconscionable-pricing ban applied only during a presidential energy emergency proclamation lasting up to 30 days at a time, covered only gasoline and other petroleum distillates, and expressly exempted futures-market transactions.
The House passed the amended bill 284-141 under a suspension-of-the-rules vote that required two-thirds: Democrats supported it 228-1 while Republicans opposed it 140-56.

The Senate received the bill on May 24, 2007 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was taken through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies and fuel sellers are better off, because no federal anti-gouging law took effect and they face no federal fines or state attorneys general suits under it; low-income households also lost the LIHEAP funding stream the penalties would have created.

for.name: Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House, where it passed as amended.

for.name: 228 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted to pass the bill, 228 to 1.

for.name: 56 of 201 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to vote for the bill.

against.name: 140 of 201 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, providing all but one of the 141 no votes.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 24, 2007 and never reported it out, so the Senate never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: House Democrats backed the bill almost unanimously, 228-1, while House Republicans opposed it 140-56; 56 Republicans broke ranks to support it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill subjects large fuel companies to civil fines of up to triple their excess profits, corporate criminal fines up to $150 million, and FTC enforcement that explicitly prioritizes companies with more than $500 million in annual fuel sales. Their interest in avoiding these penalties runs directly against consumers' interest in stable pump prices during emergencies.

industries.industry: Fuel wholesalers and retail gas stations
industries.note: Both wholesale and retail sellers are covered by the unconscionable-pricing ban, and state attorneys general could sue them directly in federal court over retail prices during declared emergencies. Sellers that genuinely faced higher costs or moved more supply would have a safe harbor under the bill's factors.

The bill bans knowingly false wholesale price reports to federal agencies, with penalties up to $1 million, but expressly exempts futures-market transactions from the gouging prohibition — so the trading of fuel contracts itself stays untouched. Trading profits built on emergency price spikes would go largely unpoliced by this bill.
